oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Examining Pay and Leadership Inequities in Educational Positions: A Critical Review Through a Care Ethics Framework
oai_dc:dc.dc:creator: Trelka, Taylor
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Women make up most of the K-12 teaching workforce in the United States but hold a smaller share of senior leadership positions and, on average, earn less than men in both teaching and administrative roles. This critical narrative literature review addresses three questions: (a) What does the literature reveal about pay and leadership disparities in K-12 education? (b) How well do common explanations account for pay and leadership disparities? and (c) How does care ethics reframe pay and leadership disparities? This review uses a critical narrative approach to interpret and evaluate evidence from economics, history, sociology, and education. Peer-reviewed studies, national datasets, and foundational works published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through ERIC, Education Source, PsycINFO, and government databases. Guided by a care ethics lens that focuses on relational responsibility and undervalued care work, the review addresses three common explanations: that men work more, that women choose lower-paying occupations, and that women are less qualified. The evidence suggests these explanations do not fully account for the disparities, which persist among educators without children, with comparable experience and credentials, and within female-dominated occupations. The literature is reframed using peer-reviewed sources while questioning potential institutional inequities. Implications for hiring, pay transparency, and negotiation practices in school districts, and directions for future research, are discussed.
